passage: The power went out halfway through the Saturday art class at the community hall, and the fans stopped. Suraj, ten, had been laughing with Jagdish sir all morning, showing off his painted kite. In the sudden dark and heat, a boy knocked a water jar over the kite. Suraj exploded, flinging his brushes and shouting. Two parents at the door muttered, "Send him home. Punish him." Jagdish sir didn't. He opened the windows for light and crouched, keeping a little distance. "That kite mattered. I'm not angry. I'm staying right here." Suraj went silent and stiff, staring at the floor. Jagdish sir stayed. After a while Suraj muttered, "Can I start again?" Sir handed him fresh paper.

qa.q: What ruined Suraj's kite painting?
qa.a: A boy knocked a water jar over the kite.

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling when he goes silent and stiff?
qa.a: He may feel scared and ashamed after exploding, unsure whether he is about to be punished or pushed away.

qa.q: Which choice of Jagdish sir's helped more than punishment would have, and why?
qa.a: He stayed calm, said the kite mattered and that he was staying, which gave Suraj a safe way back.

qa.q: Why might the parents react differently from Jagdish sir?
qa.a: They saw only the outburst and wanted a punishment, while Jagdish sir seemed to see the fear under it.

grounding: In a hot, dark hall, a ten-year-old swings from friendly to explosive to shut down, and a teacher's calm presence works better than punishment.

passage: In the Hyderabad tuition room above the chemist's shop, Naveen, eleven, was cheerful all hour, cracking jokes with Indu ma'am about her wobbly chair. Then she handed back his test with red marks and said, "Let's look at these together." His face shut like a door. He pushed the paper away, pulled his hood up and said nothing at all. Indu ma'am didn't scold. She put the paper aside. "We'll look at it when you're ready. Your joke about the chair was good." He didn't answer. The next week he came early, sat a little closer, still watching her face, and said, "Is the chair still wobbly?"

qa.q: What was Naveen joking about with Indu ma'am?
qa.a: He was joking about her wobbly chair.

qa.q: What might Naveen have been afraid of when the test came back with red marks?
qa.a: He might have feared being shamed or rejected, so he shut down to protect himself.

qa.q: What did Indu ma'am choose instead of scolding, and why did it help?
qa.a: She set the paper aside, said they would look when he was ready and praised his joke, which kept the relationship safe.

qa.q: How might Indu ma'am feel when Naveen comes early the next week?
qa.a: She may feel hopeful, seeing that her calm response made him willing to return and sit closer.

grounding: A boy shifts from friendly to shut down when corrected, and a tutor's calm, non-punishing response lets him slowly come back.

passage:
Friday. Today was a bad day again. Morning was good. Pema let me hold the class rabbit and I laughed so much. Then in maths she said, "No, like this," and took my pencil, and something in me went BOOM. I threw the pencil box and shouted that she's stupid. Everybody looked. Then I couldn't talk at all, like my mouth was locked. Sir sent me outside. I hate being sent out, it makes the boom bigger. Pema came at lunch and gave me half her paratha anyway. I didn't say thank you because I didn't know how. I want her to be my friend. I'm scared she'll stop.
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Pema give Ramesh at lunch?
qa.a: Half her paratha.

qa.q: What is Ramesh worried about at the end?
qa.a: Ramesh is scared Pema will stop being a friend, even though Ramesh wants that friendship badly.

qa.q: How could Sir respond next time instead of sending Ramesh out?
qa.a: Stay calm, give Ramesh a quiet spot nearby to settle and talk later, since being sent out makes the anger bigger.

qa.q: How might Pema feel after being called stupid and then sharing lunch?
qa.a: Pema was probably hurt but still kind, choosing to reach out again at lunch.

grounding: Shows a child who shifts from happy to explosive to shut down, wanting a friend yet fearing loss, with punishment making it worse.

passage: At the village school near Nashik, Minakshi was the first to wave at Jagdish-sir that morning, chattering about her goat's new kid. By noon, when a boy nudged her slate, she swept everything off the desk and screamed. The headmaster made her stand outside in the sun. She went silent, staring at nothing, and didn't speak for the rest of the day, not even when her friend Lata brought her water. Jagdish-sir watched her small shoulders. After the bell he sat on the step beside her, asked nothing, and said, "Tomorrow, tell me about the goat again." She shrugged. Next morning she came in, looked at him a long time, and said, "It's a girl kid."

qa.q: What did Minakshi chatter about that morning?
qa.a: Her goat's new kid.

qa.q: What might Minakshi be feeling while she stares at nothing?
qa.a: She seems shut down, probably ashamed and scared after the outburst and punishment.

qa.q: What worked better for Minakshi, the punishment or Jagdish-sir's approach, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish-sir's quiet, warm invitation worked better, because the punishment only made her shut down.

qa.q: What is it like for Lata when Minakshi won't take the water?
qa.a: Lata may feel confused and helpless, wanting to help a friend who has gone silent.

grounding: Illustrates a child switching from friendly to explosive to shut down, and how punishment deepens it while steady warmth helps.

passage: At dinner in the Rotterdam flat, Abebe was laughing, telling Sofia about the goal he'd scored. Then she asked, lightly, if he'd finished his homework. His face changed. He shoved his plate so hard it hit the wall, shouted, "You're just like all of them!" and ran to his room. Sofia's first thought was to ban football on Saturday. She didn't. She knew from the social worker's file that punishments had come fast and hard in his old homes. She cleaned up, then knocked. "I'm not angry. I'll be in the kitchen when you're ready." An hour later he came out, eyes red, and silently dried the dishes beside her.

qa.q: What did Abebe shout?
qa.a: "You're just like all of them!"

qa.q: What might Abebe be feeling when he comes out and dries the dishes?
qa.a: He seems sorry and still wary, wanting to be close to Sofia but unsure she is safe.

qa.q: Why did Sofia choose not to ban football?
qa.a: She knew harsh punishments had hurt him before and would likely deepen his mistrust, so she offered calm availability instead.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel when the plate hits the wall?
qa.a: Sofia is probably shocked and tempted to punish, then chooses patience.

grounding: Shows a child who flips from friendly to explosive and struggles to trust, with a carer avoiding punishment that would deepen it.

passage:
In the school library, Divyansh was laughing with Farhan over a comic. Then Farhan took the comic back to finish a page.
Divyansh's face changed. He shoved his chair, shouted "You always do this!" and threw the book. Then he went silent, staring at the floor, not answering anyone.
Mr Menon, the librarian, didn't send him to the principal. He said quietly, "You're safe. Come sit in the reading room with me." Divyansh went, stiff as a stick.
After some time he mumbled, "I wanted him to stay my friend." His eyes were wet.
Mr Menon told Farhan he could go back to class and thanked him for staying calm. Before the last bell, he walked Divyansh to the school counsellor, who had time to see him right away.

qa.q: What did Divyansh throw?
qa.a: The book.

qa.q: What did Divyansh seem to feel behind his outburst?
qa.a: He seemed scared of losing Farhan as a friend; he said "I wanted him to stay my friend" with wet eyes.

qa.q: Why was Mr Menon's response better than punishment?
qa.a: He calmed Divyansh, gave him a quiet safe place, and got him to the counsellor, since punishment usually deepens the mix of needing and fearing people.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the sudden change?
qa.a: Farhan was probably shocked and confused, since they had just been laughing together, and may have felt blamed for simply taking the comic back.

grounding: Shows a child who suddenly swings from friendly to explosive and then shuts down, and an adult who responds with calm instead of punishment.
